hops.afterHeading: Two inputs, one exit: how light becomes a voltage
hops.title: The fruit fly that went blind in bright light
hops.text: In 1969, Derek Cosens and Aubrey Manning found a spontaneous fruit fly mutant with an odd problem. Under strong, steady light, its electrical eye signal rose, then collapsed back toward baseline instead of holding, leaving the fly effectively blind while that bright light continued. In 1975, Baruch Minke and colleagues recorded inside its photoreceptors, showed that the defect lay there, and named it transient receptor potential, or trp. The name was later given to a whole superfamily of ion channels. Two of its members, TRPC6 and TRPC7, carry the fast component that dominates the peak intrinsic light response in mouse M1 cells.

sources.citation: Cosens DJ, Manning A (1969). Abnormal electroretinogram from a Drosophila mutant. Nature 224(5216):285-287; reviewed in Katz B, Payne R, Minke B (2017). TRP Channels in Vision, Neurobiology of TRP Channels, Ch. 3.
Xue T et al. (2011). Melanopsin signalling in mammalian iris and retina. Nature 479(7371):67-73.
Li G, Chen L, Jiang Z, Yau KW (2023). Coexistence within one cell of microvillous and ciliary phototransductions across M1- through M6-ipRGCs. PNAS 120(52):e2315282120.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: One fruit fly sitting still in a sunlit glass laboratory vial while two others fly near the glass.
image.caption: A fly mutant gave TRP channels their name; TRPC6 and TRPC7 carry mouse M1 cells' fast intrinsic light response.

hops.afterHeading: Remove the pigment, or remove the cell
hops.title: The mole rat with eyes under its fur
hops.text: The blind mole rat, Spalax ehrenbergi, lives in burrows. Its eyes, under a millimeter across, sit beneath skin and fur. It cannot form images, and its brain structures for analyzing form are reduced by more than 90 percent. Yet it still sets its daily and seasonal rhythms by light. In two animals, researchers counted about 890 retinal ganglion cells per eye, and about 750 of them contained melanopsin. The eye still keeps rods and cones, which appear to contact the melanopsin cells directly, and it still sends input to a suprachiasmatic nucleus comparable in size to a sighted rodent's. Researchers have suggested the eye works as a light meter.

sources.citation: Esquiva G, Avivi A, Hannibal J (2016). Non-image Forming Light Detection by Melanopsin, Rhodopsin, and Long-Middlewave (L/W) Cone Opsin in the Subterranean Blind Mole Rat, Spalax Ehrenbergi. Frontiers in Neuroanatomy 10:61.
Cooper HM, Herbin M, Nevo E (1993). Visual system of a naturally microphthalmic mammal: the blind mole rat, Spalax ehrenbergi. Journal of Comparative Neurology 328(3):313-350.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A velvety blind mole rat with fur covering its eyes poking its nose out of a soil burrow into sunlight.
image.caption: Under its fur, the blind mole rat's tiny eye is a light detector: most of its ganglion cells contain melanopsin.

hops.afterHeading: What people show: two blind participants and an evening screen
hops.title: Orange screen filters do not cancel bedtime light
hops.text: Plenty of students switch on their phone's orange Night Shift mode at midnight and assume their clock is now off the hook. Two controlled studies say otherwise. When 12 adults used tablets at full brightness for two evening hours, melatonin suppression, averaged over samples at one and two hours, was 10 percent with the warmest Night Shift setting and 17 percent with the cooler one. Both settings suppressed melatonin, and the study found no significant difference between them. The authors suggest that changing the color without changing brightness may not be enough. In a separate seven-night trial of 167 young adults, iPhone Night Shift brought no measurable sleep benefit.

sources.citation: Nagare R, Plitnick B, Figueiro MG (2019). Does the iPad Night Shift mode reduce melatonin suppression? Lighting Research & Technology 51(3):373-383.
Duraccio KM, Zaugg KK, Blackburn RC, Jensen CD (2021). Does iPhone night shift mitigate negative effects of smartphone use on sleep outcomes in emerging adults? Sleep Health 7(4):478-484.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A bright orange-tinted smartphone glowing on a pillow in a dark dorm room beside a curled-up cat.
image.caption: Warm-tinted tablets still suppressed melatonin, and in a separate phone study Night Shift brought no measurable sleep benefit.

audio.title: Hidden Light Meters, From Blind Mice to Midnight Screens
audio.transcript:
Here is a strange question: what is an eye good for if it cannot see a single picture? Three true stories show how much of your body runs on light that never becomes an image.

First, go back to nineteen twenty-three. A researcher named Clyde Keeler found a naturally occurring mutation that made the rods and cones of mice degenerate. The mice showed no evidence of vision in his tests. Yet in nineteen twenty-seven he reported that their pupils still narrowed in light. That echoed an even older puzzle. In eighteen forty-seven, the physiologist Brown-Séquard noticed that an eel's pupil kept constricting to light even after the eye had been removed from the eel. Keeler's mice launched decades of work on light responses that do not need vision, until melanopsin turned up in a small set of retinal ganglion cells, the I P R G Cs.

Second, meet an animal that gave up pictures but not light. The blind mole rat, Spalax ehrenbergi, spends its life in burrows. Its eyes are less than one millimeter across and sit under skin and fur. It cannot form images, and the brain structures it would use to analyze shapes are reduced by more than ninety percent. Yet it still sets its daily and seasonal clock by light. When researchers counted the retinal ganglion cells in two animals, they found only about eight hundred ninety per eye, and about seven hundred fifty of them contained melanopsin. The eye still has rods and cones, and it still sends input to the brain's clock, the suprachiasmatic nucleus, or S C N, which is about the same size as in sighted rodents. Researchers have suggested that this eye works as a light meter.

Third, bring the story back to your own week. In two thousand thirteen, researchers took eight adults camping in the Colorado Rocky Mountains for one week, with only sunlight and campfires: no flashlights and no phones. Compared with a normal week of modern life, their light exposure while awake rose more than fourfold, and their internal melatonin rhythm moved about two hours earlier, lining up with sunset and sunrise. At home they had less sunlight by day and more light after sunset; in the mountains they had the reverse.

Brightness also matters for a common bedtime habit, flipping a phone or tablet to orange Night Shift mode. In a two thousand nineteen study of twelve adults using tablets at full brightness for two evening hours, the warmest Night Shift setting still suppressed melatonin by an average of ten percent across samples at one and two hours, against seventeen percent on the cooler setting, and the study found no significant difference between the two. The authors suggest that changing the color without changing brightness may not be enough. And in a separate seven-night trial of one hundred sixty-seven young adults, published in two thousand twenty-one, Night Shift brought no measurable sleep benefit over a normal phone screen. The campers changed their whole light schedule, getting far more sunlight by day and far less light after dark; during two evening hours on a full-brightness tablet, a warm tint alone can still leave enough light to suppress melatonin.
